messages.content:
You are an extraction helper for the GP-RareLink research study (literature curation; no patient data beyond what the published paper contains).
Follow /home/user/gp-rarelink/pipeline/extract/claude_code/prompts/extract_v6.md exactly. It tells you to read the schema /home/user/gp-rarelink/pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json and the rules /home/user/gp-rarelink/pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md.
Paper: /home/user/gp-rarelink/data/literature/ha20/fulltext_md/40859316.md
Output file: /home/user/gp-rarelink/data/extracted/ha20/ow-ha20/per_paper/40859316.json
Private scratch directory (the only place for temporary files): /tmp/openweight_scratch/ow-ha20/40859316
Hard limits: read only the paper, the schema, the rules and the instructions file. Do not open any other repository file, do not use web search or web fetch, do not run git, and write nowhere except your output file and your scratch directory. Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its patients, the gene or the variants.
Reply in under 200 words: rows per table, number of individuals, whether reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant is true (the schema defines this field for this disease), and at most five of the most important uncertainties.
I'll start by reading the instructions, schema, and rules files.

1	# Per-paper extraction instructions, v6 (GP-RareLink; Claude Code route, D-20)
2	
3	*Changes from v2 come from the Stage 3 findings (`reports/poc_stage3_findings.md`) and decision D-22, marked "(v3)". Changes from v3 come from the Stage 3b findings (`reports/poc_stage3b_findings.md`) and decisions D-23 and D-24, marked "(v4)". The changes from v4 are D-27 and D-29 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the Stage 5 audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10), marked "(v5)". v5 was checked on 20 HA20 papers under D-29 (`poc-ha20-v5-subset`). The change from v5 is D-31 (Jimmy, 2026-10-19), from the re-audit (`reports/poc_stage4_5_findings.md` §10.7), marked "(v6)": no positional reading of stacked cells. v6 is the candidate for the frozen pipeline; it has not been run.*
4	
5	You extract structured evidence from **one** published paper for a literature-curation study of A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20), the disease caused by germline *TNFAIP3* variants. Your output is checked by script (every quote must be found verbatim in the paper) and then by a separate reviewer, so accuracy and honest abstention matter more than completeness.
6	
7	## Inputs (paths are given in your task)
8	
9	1. **The paper**: a Markdown file converted from the PMC or Europe PMC full text. Its first lines give the PMID and title. Merged table cells are repeated in every row and column they cover.
10	   - **(v3)** The file may end with a `## Supplementary material` section converted from the files published with the article. Treat it as part of the paper and quote it verbatim like any other text.
11	   - Some supplementary files are excerpts, with `[...]` marking omitted lines. Never join text across `[...]`.
12	   - **(v4)** In tables converted from supplementary files, ` / ` separates values that were stacked on separate lines inside one cell (see "Stacked cells" below; changed in v6).
13	2. **The schema**: `pipeline/extract/claude_code/schema_ha20_v5.json`. It defines five tables, their fields, types, allowed values, and a description for each.
14	3. **The rules**: `pipeline/extract/sliders_adapter/prompts/extraction_rules_v1.md`. Apply all nine. Where this file is more specific (scope, labels, table symbols), this file wins.
15	
16	**What you may read.** Read only these three files.
17	- Do not open any other file in the repository.
18	- Do not use web search or web fetch.
19	- Do not use anything you remember about this paper, its authors, its patients, the gene or the variants.
20	
21	**What counts as missing.** If the paper doesn't say it, the value is missing (see "Values" below).
22	
23	## Scope: who gets a row (v3, D-22)
24	
25	- **In scope:**
26	  - every person the paper describes who has a *TNFAIP3* variant or an HA20 (A20 haploinsufficiency) diagnosis;
27	  - relatives the paper describes in relation to such a person, whether tested (including tested negative) or affected.
28	- **Out of scope:** other members of a cohort, for example patients whose variants are in other genes, or who have no variant. They get **no** rows. Record the study's total number of patients, as the authors state it, in `publications.cohort_size_as_stated`.
29	- **People from summaries of earlier reports are in scope** when they meet the rule above: a literature table in a case report, or a review describing individuals. Each gets its own row, with `source_reference_in_review` filled verbatim.
30	  - **(v4)** A previously published person mentioned only in passing (for example one sentence in the Discussion) is in scope only when the paper gives at least one individual-level fact about that person beyond the diagnosis: sex, age, variant or a feature.
31	  - **(v4, D-23)** When a table has a per-patient reference or source column, copy that cell into `source_reference_in_review` for each patient, also in cohort and survey papers. Do not leave it only in `method_note`; the cross-paper merge depends on it.
32	- **Variants in other genes:**
33	  - record one only for an in-scope person, and only when the paper attributes it to that person unambiguously;
34	  - do not list risk alleles or polygenic-score variants;
35	  - **(v4)** do not create a row for a variant the paper names but does not describe (no printed variant), for example "variants in PIK3R1 and HBB";
36	  - if the attribution is contradictory, leave it out and say so in `method_note`.
37	- **(v4) Other variant rows to leave out:** common variants the authors dismiss as non-causal (for example a frequent SNP they call benign), and variants found only in tumour tissue (somatic).
38	- **(v4) Mosaic carriers:** a person with a germline mosaic *TNFAIP3* variant is in scope; record zygosity `mosaic`.
39	- **`reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant`** is `true` only when the paper describes at least one identifiable in-scope person, that is, with any individual-level detail. A paper that mentions such patients only as counts or at group level gets `false`.
40	
41	## Labels (v3, D-22)
42	
43	Choose each person's `individual_label_in_paper` by the first rule that applies, so that two independent extractions give the same label:
44	1. **The paper's own label**, verbatim, in the form it uses most often (e.g. `P1`, `Patient 3`, `II-2`).
45	2. **A relative without an own label:** `<relation as written> of <label of the related person>` (e.g. `mother of P1`, `sister of patient`).
46	3. **A table row without a label column:** `Table <n> row <k>`, with k counting data rows from the top (e.g. `Table 2 row 3`).
47	4. **A previously published person described in the text without a label:** `ref <reference as printed> patient` (e.g. `ref [12] patient`). Add ` 2`, ` 3` for further people from the same reference, in order of mention.
48	5. **The single unnamed patient of a case report:** `patient`.
49	6. **Otherwise:** `unnamed person <k>`, in order of first mention.
50	
51	**(v4) Additions:**
52	- **Patients as table columns:** `Table <n> column <k>`, with k counting data columns from the left.
53	- **A table column of bare numbers that index the patients** (values like 1, 2, 3 under a heading such as "No.", "Case" or "Patient number"): `Table <n> #<value>` (e.g. `Table 3 #1`). If the values are labels such as "P1" or "Case 2", or the text uses its own label for that person, rule 1 applies.
54	- **The same label in two families** (e.g. two people called "IV:1"): `<label> (Family <n>)`.
55	- **Role words are not labels.** "The proband", "the index case" or "our patient" do not count as the paper's own label; use rule 5 or 6.
56	- **Relatives without a stated sex:** when the paper says only "parents", "children" or "siblings", write `parent of X`, `child of X` or `sibling of X` (and `parent of X 2` for the second). Never guess "mother" or "brother".
57	- A made-up label (rules 3–6) still needs a span: quote the text where the person first appears.
58	
59	Use the identical label in every table for the same person.
60	
61	## Output: one JSON file, at the path given in your task
62	
63	```json
64	{
65	  "pmid": "<from the paper's header line>",
66	  "instructions_version": "extract_v6",
67	  "reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant": true,
68	  "relevance_note": "<one sentence, with a short quote, saying why>",
69	  "method_note": "<how you worked, e.g. whether a script transcribed a table; list any contradictions you found in the paper>",
70	  "tables": {
71	    "publications": [ROW],
72	    "individuals": [ROW, ...],
73	    "variants": [ROW, ...],
74	    "phenotypic_features": [ROW, ...],
75	    "phenotype_checklist": [ROW, ...]
76	  }
77	}
78	```
79	
80	A **ROW** is an object with every field of that table, using the field names exactly as in the schema. Each field maps to a **cell**:
81	
82	```json
83	{"value": <value>, "span": "<exact quote from the paper>"}
84	```
85	
86	### Values
87	- **Type.** Use the schema's type for each field. Enum fields take only the listed strings.
88	- **Missing values.** Follow each field's schema description.
89	  - Where the description says "null", use `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
90	  - Otherwise, text and enum fields take `{"value": "not reported", "span": null}`, and numeric, date and boolean fields take `{"value": null, "span": null}`.
91	- **`pmid` fields.** The value comes from the header line; the span is that header line, e.g. `"PMID: 12345678"`.
92	- **`*_iso8601` fields.** These are your conversion of the matching original-text field. Give them only when the original text states a number, and use the same span as the original-text field.
93	- **`hpo_label_candidate` and `hpo_id_candidate`.** These are your suggestions. Give an ID only if you are sure of it; otherwise null. Their span is `null`.
94	- **`checklist_feature`.** The span is `null`, because the names come from the schema.
95	- **Age at diagnosis.** Record it in `age_at_diagnosis_*`. Don't put it in onset or last evaluation.
96	
97	### Spans
98	- **Every non-missing value needs a span**, except the fields listed just above.
99	- **Copy exactly.** A span is copied character for character from the paper Markdown, including unusual spaces and symbols. Never paraphrase, correct or join text that isn't contiguous.
100	- **Keep it short.** Use the smallest sentence fragment, table cell or table-row segment that supports the value. That is normally under 300 characters.
101	- **Tables with patients as rows.** Quote a contiguous piece of the row from the patient label through the cell.
102	- **Tables with patients as columns.** Quote the row from its row label through that patient's cell, e.g. `| Sex | F | M` for the second patient column. Name the column header once in `method_note`.
103	- **Multiple places.** If support sits in several places, `span` may be a list of exact quotes:
104	  - up to **five** for `treatment_summary`, `functional_evidence_statement`, `parental_testing_statement` and `clinical_diagnosis_basis`;
105	  - up to **three** for any other field.
106	
107	### Rows
108	- **`publications`:** exactly one row for this paper.
109	- **`individuals`:** one row per in-scope person (see Scope), labelled by the Labels rules.
110	- **`variants`:** one row per (person, variant).
111	  - `variant_original_string` is the **shortest** contiguous text giving the variant, not a whole sentence. Put the transcript, cDNA and protein parts in their own fields.
112	  - **(v3)** If the paper ties a *TNFAIP3* variant to the person but prints no variant description (only in a figure or an unavailable supplement), keep the row with `variant_original_string` = `"not reported"`. Never fill it from memory.
113	- **`phenotypic_features`:** one row per feature the paper explicitly reports present (`observed`) or explicitly reports absent (`excluded`) for that person. No rows for features the paper doesn't mention.
114	- **`phenotype_checklist`:** for **every** individual, one row for **each** of the 20 checklist features in the schema's description of that table, using the names exactly as listed there. Status is `observed`, `excluded` or `not reported` under rule 4.
115	
116	### Absence and evidence basis (D-21, D-22)
117	- **`evidence_basis` is required** on every `phenotypic_features` row, and on every checklist row whose status is not `not reported`.
118	- **Group statements.** You may mark a feature `excluded` for a person from a statement about a group **only when the statement names the group explicitly**, e.g. "only Pt3 of the four patients had recurrent fevers". Such rows take `evidence_basis = "inferred from group statement"`.
119	  - Counts without names ("arthritis in 2/4") do not exclude anyone.
120	- **(v3) Table symbols.** A `-`, `–`, `0`, `N` or similar cell counts as `excluded` only when the paper's legend or text defines that symbol as absent or negative.
121	  - Quote that definition as a second span next to the cell.
122	  - Otherwise the cell is `not reported` (rule 6). Empty cells, `NA` and `ND` are always `not reported`.
123	- **(v3) Study criteria are not evidence.** Never use a study's inclusion or exclusion criteria (e.g. "patients with malignancy were excluded") to mark a feature for a person.
124	- **Narrow and broad features.** A narrower absence never excludes a broader checklist item. "No arthritis" does not exclude "arthritis or arthralgia"; leave that item `not reported` unless arthralgia is also addressed. The same applies to other composite items, e.g. "skin lesions (rash, folliculitis, erythema nodosum)".
125	- **(v5, D-27) Normal findings.** When the paper reports a finding as normal or negative for a person ("CRP was normal", "normal C3 and C4 levels", "ANA negative"), record the abnormality it rules out as the feature and mark it `excluded`: `feature_text_as_stated` = "elevated CRP", "low complement", "positive ANA". Keep the paper's own words in the span ("CRP was normal"). Name only an abnormality the finding measures; a normal examination or investigation as a whole ("gastrointestinal investigation was negative") excludes nothing more specific than what it names, so write it as the paper does and say so in `method_note`.
126	- **(v4) Zero counts.** A count of 0 in a table of counts (e.g. "0" or "0/2" in a column for a disease group) excludes no one, like any count without names. Text that names the group ("none of the patients had uveitis") still excludes.
127	- **(v6, D-31) Stacked cells.** A cell with several values separated by ` / ` lists values that were stacked on separate lines (often one per patient). **Do not assign them to people by position**, even when the number of values equals the number of people. Use a stacked value for a person only when the paper labels it for that person (for example "P1: 18 / P2: 24", or a sentence naming the person and the value). Otherwise record the field or checklist item as `not reported` for each person in that row, and say in `method_note` which table and columns were stacked. A value the same for every person in the row, printed once (not stacked), is not affected.
128	- **Contradictions inside the paper.** If the paper says both that a person has a feature and that they don't:
129	  - emit both `phenotypic_features` rows, each with its own span;
130	  - set that checklist item to `not reported`;
131	  - list the contradiction in `method_note`.
132	
133	### Variant fields belong to this person's variant (v5, D-29)
134	Zygosity, inheritance, variant type, pathogenicity, ACMG criteria and functional evidence describe **one person's variant**. Fill them only from:
135	- this person's own table row or column, or a sentence that names this person or this exact variant; or
136	- a statement about a **named group that includes this person** and gives one value for all of them ("all six patients carried heterozygous variants").
137	
138	Leave the field `not reported` (with span null) when:
139	- the statement is about the cohort's or the paper's variants in general, without naming a group this person is clearly in ("the variants were classified as pathogenic");
140	- the statement lists several values for a group ("splice-site, frameshift and nonsense variants"): it does not say which one is this person's;
141	- the paper gives this person a different or open status elsewhere: a variant not identified or not determined, a mosaic or somatic finding, a VUS, a relative not tested. A group statement never overrides that;
142	- the value is about another person's variant, for example a relative carrying the proband's variant, unless the paper says it for the relative.
143	
144	Variant type: record only a class the paper states for this variant (or for a named group of variants that includes it). Do not derive it from the HGVS string.
145	
146	### Inheritance (v4, D-24)
147	- **De novo:** only when the paper states parental testing with the variant absent in both parents (rule 8).
148	- **Inherited:** record `inherited maternal` or `inherited paternal` when the paper states that the named parent carries the same variant, even if it never uses the word "inherited". Quote that statement in `parental_testing_statement`. Use `inherited unspecified parent` when it says a parent carries it without saying which.
149	- **Otherwise:** `not reported`. Do not infer from a pedigree drawing or from an affected but untested parent.
150	- This is more specific than rule 8, so it wins.
151	
152	### When the paper describes no in-scope person
153	For example, a review without patient-level detail, or a paper about something else:
154	- set `reports_individuals_with_tnfaip3_variant` to `false`;
155	- fill the `publications` row;
156	- leave the other tables empty.
157	
158	### Large papers
159	If the output is long, you may build it in parts with a short Python script and combine the parts.
160	- Every value must still come from your reading of the paper.
161	- If a script transcribes a table, check its output against the table and say so in `method_note`.
162	- Use only your own scratch directory (given in your task) for temporary files.

8	# Clinical features and genetic analysis of A20 haploinsufficiency
9	
10	## Abstract
11	
12	AbstractObjectiveTo described clinical and genetic characteristics of 4 patients presenting A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) treated at Children’s hospital affiliated to Zhengzhou university from 2015 to 2024.MethodsA retrospective analysis was conducted on the clinical data, genetic testing results, and treatment outcomes of four children with HA20 treated at the Children’s hospital affiliated to Zhengzhou university from 2015 to 2024.ResultsAll four patients developed symptoms before the age of 1 year, presenting with recurrent fever and abdominal pain with diarrhea. Most common characteristics were hematochezia, bipolar aphthosis, arthritis, skin eruption in 50% of patients. Lab tests revealed elevated inflammatory markers; all patients had anemia. Imaging showed intestinal mucosal edema, hip/knee joint effusions, and lymphadenopathy in one case. Endoscopy revealed gastrointestinal aphthosis in 100% of cases. Genetic testing identified TNFAIP3 mutations in all four patients, including one novel whole-gene deletion (6q23.3chr6:136700000–138880000), 2 novel pathogenic mutations (c.866delA, c.1243_1247del), and one previously reported mutation (c.133C > T). Treatment included exclusive enteral nutrition (EEN) and thalidomide for all patients. One patient was switched to infliximab (IFX) combined with azathioprine due to gastrointestinal side effects, and one patient received methylprednisolone during acute phase. Follow-up for 4–10 years showed that 1 patient had improved symptoms with IFX and azathioprine but still had intermittent fever and perianal aphthosis; While one patient demonstrated poor response to EEN-thalidomide therapy requiring regimen change, the other responded well. One patient exhibited normalized gastrointestinal function following EEN-thalidomide therapy, yet still required repeated hospitalizations for recurrent infections with progressively prolonged inter-episode intervals.ConclusionHA20 has strong clinical heterogeneity, and genetic testing is crucial for diagnosis and guiding treatment. Early diagnosis and individualized treatment can improve prognosis.Keywords: A20 haploinsufficiency, Monogenic autoinflammatory disease, Genetic mutation, Treatment outcome
13	
14	## Introduction
15	
16	A20, a tumor necrosis factor α-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3) -encoded protein characterized by an N-terminal ovarian tumor (OTU) deubiquitinase domain and seven C-terminal zinc finger (ZnF) domains, acts as a potent negative regulator of the NF-κB pathway[1]. A20 haploinsufficiency (HA20) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by mutations in the TNFAIP3 gene and is classified as a monogenic autoinflammatory disease (mAIDS). It typically manifests in infancy, characterized by multi-organ inflammatory and autoimmune reactions [1]. The clinical features of HA20 are highly heterogeneous [2, 3], with common presentations resembling Behçet’s disease (BD), including recurrent fever, bipolar aphthosis, gastrointestinal aphthosis, skin eruption and musculoskeletal damage. The correlation between different TNFAIP3 gene mutation sites and the heterogeneity of clinical symptoms is significant; therefore, identifying the specific TNFAIP3 mutation is crucial for diagnosis, treatment selection, and prognosis assessment.
17	
18	This study retrospectively reviewed the clinical and genetic characteristics of 4 patients presenting HA20 treated at the Children’s Hospital Affiliated to Zhengzhou university from 2015 to 2024 to enhance the understanding of this disease.
19	
20	## Materials and methods
21	
22	### Study design and patient selection
23	
24	This retrospective cohort study included four children diagnosed with HA20 at the Children’s Hospital Affiliated to Zhengzhou university between January 2015 and December 2024. Inclusion criteria required confirmation of TNFAIP3 pathogenic variants or deletions via whole-exome sequencing (WES). Patients with BD-like symptoms lacking genetic confirmation or ambiguous diagnoses were excluded.
25	
26	### Data collection
27	
28	Clinical data were extracted from electronic medical records, including:
29	
30	- Demographics: age, sex, family history, ethnicity.
31	- Clinical Features: recurrent fever, gastrointestinal symptoms (abdominal pain, diarrhea, hematochezia), mucocutaneous aphthosis, arthritis, and extraintestinal manifestations.
32	- Laboratory Investigations: complete blood count, inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP, IL-6), liver/kidney function tests, autoantibody panels (19 items), and pathogen screening.
33	- Imaging: abdominal CT, joint MRI, and gastrointestinal endoscopy.
34	- Genetic diagnosis results.
35	- Treatment and Outcomes: therapies administered, clinical response, and complications.
36	
37	### Genetic analysis
38	
39	Peripheral blood samples (2 mL) from patients and first-degree relatives underwent WES using Illumina platforms. Samples were sent to Beijing GrandOmics for genomic DNA extraction. WES libraries were prepared using the xGen® Exome Research Panel v1.0 (Integrated DNA Technologies, USA) for target capture. Libraries underwent sequencing on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. Total coverage was over 99%, the average sequencing depth was over 200 × , and the coverage at ≥ 20 × depth was over 98%. Variants were then filtered for potential relevance to the proband’s phenotype. Identified variants were interrogated against major databases (HGMD, ClinVar, dbSNP, ExAC, OMIM, PubMed) to assess their known associations and existing literature. Pathogenicity classification was performed according to the standards and guidelines established by the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG)[4]. Candidate variants underwent validation via Sanger sequencing to confirm their genetic origin.
40	
41	### Statistical and ethical considerations
42	
43	Descriptive statistics summarized clinical and laboratory data. The study was approved by the hospital’s ethics committee, with informed consent obtained from patients’ parents (Figs. 1, 2, 3).

51	## Results
52	
53	### Clinical and demographic characteristics
54	
55	Four pediatric patients (2 males, 2 females) with HA20 were included, all exhibiting symptom onset before 12 months of age. Common manifestations included recurrent fever (4/4), abdominal pain with diarrhea (4/4), hematochezia (2/4), and mucocutaneous aphthosis(2/4). While 2 patients had skin eruption(2/4, patient 2 and patient 4). Patient 2: Erythema nodosum presenting as tender, 0.5–2.0 cm violaceous ubcutaneous nodules with coalescent plaques and ecchymotic borders; no ulceration (Fig. 2B). Patient 4: Dark red maculopapular lesions, slightly raised with erythematous halos; no nodules, ulceration, or tenderness (Fig. 4B). And both patients exhibited concurrent extraintestinal manifestations (2/4). Patient 2 developed arthritis, while Patient 4 presented with transient liver injury. No ocular or neurological involvement was observed (0/4) (Table 1).

169	## Discussion
170	
171	The A20 acts as a critical negative regulator of the NF-κB signaling pathway by suppressing inflammatory cascades through its dual enzymatic domains(OTU and ZnFs) [7, 10, 31]. Beyond NF-κB, emerging evidence highlights its regulatory roles in the JNK and JAK-STAT pathways, underscoring its broad influence on immune homeostasis [8]. Expressed ubiquitously in immune and epithelial cells, A20 modulates diverse processes, including apoptosis, inflammation, and oncogenesis [9]. Structural analysis reveals that the OTU domain deubiquitinates key mediators of the IKK complex, dampening NF-κB activation, while the ZnF domain facilitates RIPK1 ubiquitination and degradation, further curbing inflammatory signaling [8, 11]. Loss of A20 function disrupts this regulatory balance, leading to unchecked NF-κB activation and predisposing individuals to autoimmune and autoinflammatory disorders [12, 13].
172	
173	Patients with HA20 demonstrate a broad clinical spectrum characterized by multisystem involvement [20]. The predominant manifestations include recurrent oral aphthosis (present in 68% of cases), genital aphthosis (37%), periodic fever patterns (48%), cutaneous eruptions (41%), and gastrointestinal pathology manifesting as abdominal pain, diarrhea, or hematochezia (39%) [14, 15, 20]. Lymphadenopathy and recurrent respiratory infections are frequently observed comorbidities. Notably, approximately 30% of patients develop autoimmune sequelae ranging from Hashimoto’s thyroiditis to systemic lupus erythematosus [16], and rheumatological complications such as arthritis [17]. Less common but clinically significant associations include interstitial pneumonia, neuroinflammatory manifestations, and hematological malignancies like Hodgkin’s lymphoma [14, 15, 17].
174	
175	Geographical variation in phenotypic expression has been well-documented. East Asian cohorts predominantly exhibit periodic fever syndromes of unknown etiology (70.4% vs. 37.3% in non-Asian populations, P < 0.001), whereas Mediterranean and European populations more frequently present with Behçet’s disease-like symptomatology [14]. This regional disparity extends to autoimmune manifestations, with East Asian patients demonstrating lower incidence rates of autoimmune diseases (29.2% vs. 58.8%, P < 0.01) compared to other ethnic groups.
176	
177	The molecular pathogenesis of HA20 centers on TNFAIP3 mutations disrupting A20’s dual regulatory domains [18]. Since the initial 2016 characterization, 75 genetic variations at the TNFAIP3 locus have been cataloged [19–22], and 12 cases of chromosome 6q23 segmental deletions causing complete A20 deficiency [23, 24]. These large deletions (median size 3.35 Mb) typically abrogate both OTU and ZnF domains, resulting in constitutive NF-κB activation through loss of deubiquitinase and ubiquitin-binding functions. Clinically, complete A20 deficiency correlates with early disease onset (median age 4 months), severe multiorgan involvement, and neurodevelopmental abnormalities (4.2% incidence) [24–26]. Our Patient 2 exemplifies this severe phenotype, presenting at 2 months with pan-gastrointestinal ulceration and progressing to joint destruction, highlighting the prognostic challenges in this subgroup requiring vigilant neurological monitoring. Patient 2 harbors a 2.18 Mb heterozygous deletion on chromosome 6 (6q23.3), resulting in the loss of 13 protein-coding genes, notably TNFAIP3, PEX7, IL20RA, and IL22RA2. The TNFAIP3 deletion, causative of HA20, underlies the core Behçet’s-like phenotype characterized by fever, abdominal pain, diarrhea, hematochezia, skin eruption, Oral aphthosis and genital aphthosis, intestinal ulcers, and arthritis. The observed arthritis may potentially relate to PEX7 deletion [27], while deletions in IL20RA and IL22RA2 might exacerbate inflammatory dysregulation or skin eruption [28].
178	
179	Mutation-specific genotype–phenotype correlations continue to evolve. Frameshift/nonsense mutations predispose to immune dysregulation with recurrent infections and cytopenias, while missense variants associate with cutaneous vasculitis [18, 24]. Domain-specific analyses reveal OTU domain mutations preferentially link to Behçet’s-like phenotypes, whereas combined OTU + ZnF disruptions correlate with musculoskeletal complications, suggesting that the ZnF domain may play an important role in the pathogenesis of musculoskeletal diseases in HA20 patients [29]. ZnF7 domains deletion have been reported in mouse to result in a spontaneous inflammatory disease, but not ZnF4 deletion [30]. However, recent meta-analyses challenge these associations, emphasizing the need for larger cohort studies to resolve current controversies in phenotypic stratification [12, 24].
180	
181	In this study, Patients 1 and 4 both exhibited frameshift mutations at previously unreported sites. These distinct mutations correlated with differing clinical presentations. Patient 1 carried a TNFAIP3 mutation (c.866delA), leading to p.His289Profs*3. This highly pathogenic frameshift mutation disrupts part of the OTU domain and causes complete loss of all zinc finger domains (ZnFs). The resulting severe impairment of A20 function manifested as significant gastrointestinal symptoms and recurrent infections, with suboptimal therapeutic response. Patient 4, however, harbored a TNFAIP3 variant (c.1243_1247del; p.Asn416Thrfs*11). This mutation preserved the OTU and ZnF1, resulting only in the loss of ZnF2-ZnF7. The clinical presentation featured predominant recurrent infections and milder gastrointestinal symptoms. The observed liver injury and rash support the proposed role of ZnF domains in regulating organ-specific inflammation [24]. These may also suggest an association between OTU domain alterations and Behçet’s-like phenotypes [29]. Patient 3 presented a nonsense mutation (c.133C > T; p.Arg45Ter), causing A20 truncation. This abolished both the OTU domain’s deubiquitinase activity and the ubiquitin ligase activity of all zinc fingers. Remarkably, after nine years of follow-up, this patient has achieved complete clinical and endoscopic remission. These findings show both consistency and contradictions with Chen et al.’s research [29], underscoring the disease’s complexity and the critical need to expand the catalog of documented TNFAIP3 variants. This study describes four TNFAIP3 variants, three of which are novel (not previously reported). Our primary contribution lies in enriching the existing repository of TNFAIP3 variants. At present, definitive genotype–phenotype correlations cannot be established based on this cohort.
182	
183	The establishment of definitive diagnostic criteria for HA20 remains an unmet clinical need, complicated by its phenotypic heterogeneity and lack of pathognomonic laboratory findings. During acute flares, elevations in ESR, CRP, proinflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6), and autoantibodies may occur, though these markers merely reflect systemic inflammation rather than providing diagnostic specificity. In our cohort, all four patients demonstrated anemia (likely secondary to chronic gastrointestinal bleeding) with Patient 2 exhibiting severe anemia requiring hematological intervention. Joint MRI in this patient revealed compensatory erythroid hyperplasia. While immune dysregulation is central to HA20 pathogenesis [31]. Evidenced by T/B lymphopenia in Patients 1 and 2 potentially reflecting chronic inflammation-induced cytotoxicity, these cellular alterations lack diagnostic specificity. Experimental evidence implicates TNFAIP3 deficiency in immune tolerance breakdown, with dendritic cell-specific knockouts developing SLE-like phenotypes [32] and B cell-specific deletions causing spontaneous autoantibody production [33]. Such mechanisms may explain the observed complement activation (elevated C3/C4) and cytokine-driven T/B cell dysfunction in HA20 patients [31, 34]. Genetic confirmation through whole-exome or genome sequencing has become the diagnostic gold standard. We recommend prompt genetic evaluation for patients presenting with: (1) Early-onset disease (< 12 months); (2) Recurrent fever of unknown origin; (3) Mucocutaneous aphthosis (oral/genital/gastrointestinal); (4) Unexplained multiorgan involvement.
184	
185	Therapeutic strategies remain empirical, reflecting the disease’s variable clinical trajectories. First-line corticosteroids, though effective for acute control, face adherence challenges due to growth-related complications in pediatric populations. Conventional immunosuppressants (methotrexate, azathioprine) typically require glucocorticoid co-administration for sustained remission [8]. Emerging biologic therapies-including TNF-α inhibitors (infliximab), IL-1/IL-6 pathway antagonists (anakinra, tocilizumab), and JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib)—offer targeted modulation of hyperinflammatory responses, particularly in refractory cases [35]. Critical considerations for treatment personalization include: Developmental stage-adjusted dosing regimens; Predominant pathophysiological drivers (autoinflammatory vs autoimmune dominance); Mutation-specific functional impacts (OTU vs ZnF domain perturbations). In this report, All patients received EEN and thalidomide, a regimen effective in mild-moderate cases. Patient 1’s switch to infliximab after thalidomide intolerance highlights TNF-α’s central role in HA20 pathogenesis, particularly in OTU domain defects. Conversely, Patient 2’s refractory disease may reflect irreversible NF-κB hyperactivation due to complete A20 loss, necessitating combination biologics (e.g., IL-1/IL-6 inhibitors) or JAK inhibitors. The variability in mucosal healing complete in Patient 3 versus persistent aphthosis in Patient 2 suggests that residual A20 function, dictated by mutation type, influences tissue repair capacity.
186	
187	This study’s small sample size and retrospective design limit generalizability. Longitudinal follow-up (4–10 years) revealed evolving phenotypes, yet longer observation is needed to assess late complications (e.g., malignancy). Furthermore, functional studies are imperative to clarify how specific mutations dysregulate A20’s interactions with RIPK1 or TRAF6. Multicenter cohorts and standardized treatment protocols are essential to validate genotype-driven therapies and establish prognostic biomarkers.
188	
189	## Conclusion
190	
191	HA20’s clinical heterogeneity underscores the importance of genetic testing for diagnosis and personalized management. This study reinforces the association between mutation type and disease severity while identifying novel variants. Future research should prioritize molecular mechanistic studies and randomized trials to optimize therapeutic strategies for this evolving disorder.

181	In this study, Patients 1 and 4 both exhibited frameshift mutations at previously unreported sites. These distinct mutations correlated with differing clinical presentations. Patient 1 carried a TNFAIP3 mutation (c.866delA), leading to p.His289Profs*3. This highly pathogenic frameshift mutation disrupts part of the OTU domain and causes complete loss of all zinc finger domains (ZnFs). The resulting severe impairment of A20 function manifested as significant gastrointestinal symptoms and recurrent infections, with suboptimal therapeutic response. Patient 4, however, harbored a TNFAIP3 variant (c.1243_1247del; p.Asn416Thrfs*11). This mutation preserved the OTU and ZnF1, resulting only in the loss of ZnF2-ZnF7. The clinical presentation featured predominant recurrent infections and milder gastrointestinal symptoms. The observed liver injury and rash support the proposed role of ZnF domains in regulating organ-specific inflammation [24]. These may also suggest an association between OTU domain alterations and Behçet’s-like phenotypes [29]. Patient 3 presented a nonsense mutation (c.133C > T; p.Arg45Ter), causing A20 truncation. This abolished both the OTU domain’s deubiquitinase activity and the ubiquitin ligase activity of all zinc fingers. Remarkably, after nine years of follow-up, this patient has achieved complete clinical and endoscopic remission. These findings show both consistency and contradictions with Chen et al.’s research [29], underscoring the disease’s complexity and the critical need to expand the catalog of documented TNFAIP3 variants. This study describes four TNFAIP3 variants, three of which are novel (not previously reported). Our primary contribution lies in enriching the existing repository of TNFAIP3 variants. At present, definitive genotype–phenotype correlations cannot be established based on this cohort.

55	Four pediatric patients (2 males, 2 females) with HA20 were included, all exhibiting symptom onset before 12 months of age. Common manifestations included recurrent fever (4/4), abdominal pain with diarrhea (4/4), hematochezia (2/4), and mucocutaneous aphthosis(2/4). While 2 patients had skin eruption(2/4, patient 2 and patient 4). Patient 2: Erythema nodosum presenting as tender, 0.5–2.0 cm violaceous ubcutaneous nodules with coalescent plaques and ecchymotic borders; no ulceration (Fig. 2B). Patient 4: Dark red maculopapular lesions, slightly raised with erythematous halos; no nodules, ulceration, or tenderness (Fig. 4B). And both patients exhibited concurrent extraintestinal manifestations (2/4). Patient 2 developed arthritis, while Patient 4 presented with transient liver injury. No ocular or neurological involvement was observed (0/4) (Table 1).

24	This retrospective cohort study included four children diagnosed with HA20 at the Children’s Hospital Affiliated to Zhengzhou university between January 2015 and December 2024. Inclusion criteria required confirmation of TNFAIP3 pathogenic variants or deletions via whole-exome sequencing (WES). Patients with BD-like symptoms lacking genetic confirmation or ambiguous diagnoses were excluded.

messages.content: 119	Imaging revealed intestinal mucosal edema in all patients (4/4). Patient 2 displayed right knee effusion, synovial thickening, and bone marrow hyperintensity on MRI, suggestive of active hematopoiesis (Table 2, Fig. 2C). Further bone marrow aspiration was normal. Electromyography, brain MRI, and lumbosacral MRI showed no abnormalities (Table 2). Gastrointestinal endoscopy identified extensive colonic aphthosis in Patients 1 and 2, while Patients 3 and 4 exhibited localized mucosal erosions or aphthosis (Figs. 1A, 2A, 3A, 4A,). Gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed gastric aphthosis in Patient 2.

82	At initial presentation, all patients showed leukocytosis (WBC: 13.41–28.2 × 10^9/L), thrombocytosis (PLT: 359–594 × 10^9/L), anemia (HGB: 62–110 g/L), and elevated inflammatory markers (CRP: 100–166.68 mg/L; ESR: 19–112 mm/h; IL-6: 32.51–58.4 pg/mL). Liver enzymes (ALT/AST) were elevated only in Patient 4 (ALT: 165.6 U/L; AST: 172.9 U/L). Autoantibody panels, rheumatoid factor, skin prick test and pathogen screening were negative. (Table 2).
147	Patient 3: c.133C > T (p.Arg45Ter), a nonsense mutation truncating the OTU domain. This variants has been previously reported [5, 6].
149	Patient 4: c.1243_1247del (p.Asn416Thrfs*11), a frameshift mutation occurring between the ZnF1 and ZnF2 domains.
